title: Peter Pan
author: J. M. Barrie
ru: Мальчик, который не хочет взрослеть, уносит Венди и её братьев в Нетландию — к феям, русалкам и пиратам капитана Крюка.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Boy at the Window
chapters.text:
All children, except one, grow up. This is the story of that one boy.

The Darlings lived in a tall, narrow house in London. Mr Darling worked in an office in the city and worried about money all the time. Mrs Darling was kind and pretty, and she had a secret kiss at the corner of her mouth. Nobody could ever get it, not even Mr Darling.

There were three children: Wendy, the oldest, then John, and little Michael. Their nurse was not a woman. She was a big black-and-white dog called Nana. The Darlings could not pay for a real nurse, so Nana did the job, and she did it very well. She walked the children to school, carried an umbrella in her mouth when it rained, and never let anyone go to bed with wet feet.

Every night Mrs Darling sat in the nursery, the children's bedroom, and told them stories. She did not know that somebody else was listening. Outside the window, in the dark, a boy was listening too.

One night she fell asleep by the fire. A cold wind woke her. The window was open, and a strange boy was standing in the room. He was wearing clothes made of leaves, and his face was full of laughter. A tiny ball of light was flying round and round his head.

Mrs Darling screamed. Nana ran in and jumped at the boy. He was out of the window in a second, but Nana pushed it shut so fast that it caught his shadow. The boy got away. His shadow didn't.

Mrs Darling picked it up. It was thin and grey and quite ordinary. She rolled it up carefully and put it in a drawer.

“He will come back for it,” she thought, and she felt afraid.

A week later, on a snowy Friday, Mr and Mrs Darling were getting ready to go out to dinner. Michael did not want to take his medicine.

“Be a man, Michael,” said Mr Darling.

“You take yours first, Father,” said Michael. “Your medicine is in the cupboard.”

Mr Darling's medicine was much worse than Michael's. “All right,” he said. “We'll take it together. One, two, three!”

Michael drank his. Mr Darling quickly hid his glass behind his back.

“Father!” cried Wendy.

Then Mr Darling had an idea, a very silly one. He poured his medicine into Nana's bowl of milk. “It's just a joke,” he laughed.

Nana drank it. Then she looked at him with sad eyes and walked slowly back to her kennel. Nobody laughed. Mr Darling felt foolish, and when he felt foolish, he always got angry.

“That dog is not staying in the nursery tonight!” he shouted. He pulled Nana down to the yard and tied her up.

Mrs Darling lit the three little night-lights and kissed the children goodnight.

“Can anything hurt us now, Mother?” asked Wendy.

“Nothing, my darlings. The night-lights are a mother's eyes. They watch over you while she is away.”

Then she followed her husband out into the snowy street.

In the yard, Nana barked and barked. In the nursery, the children slept. And then, one by one, the three night-lights went out.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. A Shadow and a Thimble
chapters.text:
Something bright flew in through the window. It was not a night-light. It was a fairy, no bigger than your hand, and her name was Tinker Bell. When she spoke, it sounded like tiny golden bells.

A moment later the boy flew in after her.

“Tink, where is it?” he whispered.

Tink rang her answer: in the big drawer. The boy pulled out his shadow and was so happy that he shut the drawer again with Tink still inside it.

Now he had his shadow, but how could he put it back on? He tried to stick it to his feet with soap from the bathroom. It didn't work. The shadow just lay on the floor. The boy sat down and cried.

The crying woke Wendy. She sat up in bed. She was not frightened. She was interested.

“Boy,” she said politely, “why are you crying?”

He jumped up and bowed to her, very grandly. Wendy bowed back from the bed.

“What's your name?” he asked.

“Wendy Moira Angela Darling. What's yours?”

“Peter Pan.”

“Is that all?”

“Yes,” he said, and for the first time he felt it was rather a short name.

Wendy saw the shadow and the soap. “You can't stick it on with soap, silly,” she said. “I'll sew it on for you.” She took out her sewing box and sewed the shadow to his feet. It hurt a little, but Peter didn't cry this time.

Soon the shadow was dancing across the floor with him.

“How clever I am!” Peter shouted. “Oh, the cleverness of me!”

“And I did nothing, I suppose?” said Wendy.

“You did a little,” said Peter, still dancing.

Wendy offered him a kiss. Peter held out his hand. He didn't know what a kiss was! So Wendy kindly put a thimble in his hand, the little metal hat that you wear on your finger when you sew. Peter thought it was a kiss and gave her one of his buttons in return. It was an acorn. Wendy put it on a chain around her neck.

“How old are you, Peter?”

“I don't know. I ran away on the day I was born. My mother and father were talking about what I would be when I was a man. I don't want to be a man! I want always to be a little boy and to have fun.”

He lived in Neverland, he said, with the Lost Boys: boys who fell out of their prams, their baby carriages, when their nurses were looking the other way.

“Are there no girls?”

“Oh no. Girls are much too clever to fall out of their prams.”

Wendy liked that very much.

Just then they heard angry bells from the drawer. Peter let Tink out. She flew round Wendy's head, ringing furiously.

“She says you're a great ugly girl,” Peter explained. Tink was jealous.

“Wendy,” Peter said, “the Lost Boys have no mother and nobody tells them stories. Come with me! You can tell us stories and tuck us into bed at night.”

“Oh, I'd love to! But I can't fly.”

“I'll teach you.”

Wendy jumped out of bed. “John! Michael! Wake up! There's a boy here, and he's going to teach us to fly!”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Second to the Right
chapters.text:
John and Michael were awake in a second.

“It's easy,” said Peter. “You just think lovely, happy thoughts, and they lift you up into the air.”

The children thought about Christmas and cake and birthdays. They jumped off their beds and landed on the floor, bump, bump, bump.

Peter laughed. Of course, happy thoughts were not enough. Nobody can fly without a little fairy dust. He blew some over each of them.

“Now move your shoulders like this,” he said, “and let go.”

Michael went first, and suddenly he was floating across the room. “I'm flying!” he screamed. A minute later all three of them were flying round the nursery and bumping into the ceiling.

“Let's go out!” cried John.

“There are pirates in Neverland,” Peter said.

“Pirates!” John took his Sunday hat. “Let's go at once!”

In the yard, Nana was pulling and pulling at her chain. At last it broke, and she ran through the snow to find Mr and Mrs Darling. They all hurried home and ran up the stairs. But they were too late. The window was open, the beds were empty, and far away, above the roofs of London, four small shapes were flying towards the stars.

“Which way is Neverland?” Wendy asked.

“Second to the right,” said Peter, “and straight on till morning.”

They flew over towns and seas, by night and by day. When they were hungry, Peter took food from the mouths of birds. When Michael fell asleep, he dropped like a stone, and Peter caught him just above the waves. Peter thought this was a great joke. Worse, he sometimes flew off for an adventure and came back without remembering who they were. Wendy began to feel a little afraid.

Then one morning Peter said, “There it is.”

Below them lay an island with green forests, a blue lagoon and a tall ship on a dark river.

“Pirates,” said Peter quietly. “Their captain is Hook. He has an iron hook instead of a right hand, and he tears at people with it.”

BOOM!

The pirates' big gun, Long Tom, fired at them. The children were thrown across the sky in different directions. Wendy found herself alone with Tinker Bell.

“Follow me,” Tink's bells seemed to say. And Wendy did.

Down in the forest, the Lost Boys were waiting for Peter. There were six of them, all dressed in animal skins: Tootles, Nibs, Slightly, Curly and the Twins. Tink flew down to them first.

“Peter wants you to shoot the Wendy bird,” she rang.

The boys looked up. A big white bird was flying above the trees.

“Quick, Tootles!” cried the others. “Peter will be so pleased!”

Tootles took his bow and arrow and shot. The Wendy bird fell from the sky and lay still on the grass with an arrow in her chest.

Tootles stood over her, very proud. “I shot the Wendy bird!”

Then they heard Peter's happy voice above them.

“Great news, boys! At last I've brought you a mother!”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The House Under the Ground
chapters.text:
Nobody answered. Peter landed and looked at their faces.

“Where is she?”

The boys stepped back. Wendy was lying on the grass.

Peter pulled the arrow out of her and turned to the boys. “Whose arrow is this?”

“Mine, Peter,” said Tootles, and he went down on his knees. “Strike me, Peter. I deserve it.”

Peter lifted the arrow. But he couldn't do it.

Then Nibs cried, “Look! She's moving! The Wendy lady is alive!”

Peter knelt down beside her. The arrow didn't reach her heart. It hit the acorn button on her chain.

“It's my kiss!” said Peter. “My kiss saved her life!”

Above their heads they heard tiny, angry bells. It was Tink. She was crying because Wendy was alive.

“Tink told us to shoot,” said Curly.

Peter looked up angrily. “Tinker Bell, I'm not your friend any more. Go away for ever!”

Tink flew off, crying. But Wendy lifted her arm a little, and Peter said, “Well, not for ever. For a whole week.”

They could not carry Wendy into their home under the ground, so they built a little house around her. It had red walls, a mossy roof and a door with a knocker. John and Michael found them at last and helped. John's Sunday hat became the chimney, and soon smoke was coming out of it.

At last Peter knocked politely on the door. Wendy opened it.

“Wendy lady,” said the boys, “please be our mother.”

“I'm only a little girl,” said Wendy. “I have no real experience.”

“That doesn't matter,” said Peter. “We only need a nice motherly person.”

“Oh dear,” said Wendy. “I think that's exactly what I am.”

Soon Wendy was well again, and she moved into the boys' home under the ground.

The Lost Boys lived under the ground. Each boy had his own hollow tree, and he slid down it into a big room with a fire. Wendy cooked their dinners, mended their socks and put them to bed. And every night she told them stories.

Not far away, on the dark river, lay the pirate ship, the Jolly Roger. Its captain was James Hook. He had long black curls and blue eyes, and his manners were beautiful, even when he was being cruel. The pirates were afraid of him. And Hook was afraid of only one thing.

“The crocodile,” he said one evening, as he walked through the forest with Smee, his fat little pirate. “Pan cut off my right hand and threw it to a crocodile. The crocodile liked the taste so much that it follows me from sea to sea, hoping to eat the rest of me.”

“But you always hear it coming, Captain,” said Smee.

That was true. The crocodile once swallowed a clock, and now, wherever it went, the clock went with it. Tick-tock, tick-tock.

“One day,” said Smee, “the clock will stop. And then...”

Hook went pale. “Yes. That's what I'm afraid of.”

Just then he heard a sound. Tick-tock, tick-tock.

Hook jumped. “Run!” he cried. As he hurried back to his ship, he looked over his shoulder.

“Peter Pan,” he whispered. “One day I'll get you.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Mermaids' Lagoon
chapters.text:
Life in Neverland was full of adventures, but the best of all happened on the Mermaids' Lagoon.

On sunny days the mermaids sat on a big rock in the middle of the water, combing their long hair. They played with Peter, but they splashed Wendy with their tails and laughed at her.

One afternoon the children were lying on that rock, which was called Marooners' Rock. Wendy was sewing, and the boys were asleep. Suddenly the sun went in. The water turned cold and grey.

Peter jumped up. “Pirates!” he whispered. “Into the water!”

The children dived in and hid. A small boat came across the lagoon. Two pirates were in it, Smee and Starkey, and a prisoner. It was Tiger Lily, the brave princess of the island's people. Her hands and feet were tied.

“We'll leave her on the rock,” said Smee. “When the water comes up, she'll drown.”

Tiger Lily said nothing. She was too proud to cry.

Peter did not want her to die. So he did a very clever thing. He made his voice sound exactly like Hook's.

“Ahoy there, you fools!” he called across the water.

“It's the Captain!” said Starkey. “He must be swimming out to us.”

“Set the princess free,” said the voice.

“Free, Captain?”

“Yes, cut her ropes, or I'll put my hook in you!”

The pirates cut the ropes, and Tiger Lily slid into the water like an eel.

Then they heard another voice: “Boat ahoy!” It was the real Hook. He swam to the boat and climbed in.

“Where's the princess?”

“We let her go, Captain. You told us to.”

Hook went white. “Spirit of this dark lagoon,” he called, “do you hear me?”

“I hear you,” answered Peter, in Hook's voice.

“Who are you?”

“I'm James Hook, captain of the Jolly Roger!”

“You are not!” shouted Hook. “Are you a man?”

“No!”

“A boy?”

“Yes!”

“An ordinary boy?”

“No! A wonderful boy!” And then Peter couldn't stop himself. “I'm Peter Pan!”

The boys swam out to help him, and in a moment there was a terrible fight in the water. Peter and Hook met on the rock. Peter was higher up than Hook. That wasn't fair, Peter thought, so he held out his hand to help Hook up. And Hook clawed him with his iron hook.

It hurt, but the unfairness hurt Peter more. He could only stare.

Then — tick-tock, tick-tock. Hook jumped into the water and swam away as fast as he could, with the crocodile behind him.

Now Peter and Wendy were alone on the rock. Peter was hurt and could not fly. Wendy was too tired to swim. And the water was coming up.

Just then a kite came flying past. It was Michael's. The wind took it from his hands a few days before. Peter caught its tail. “It can carry one of us,” he said. Before Wendy could argue, he tied it round her, and the kite carried her away over the lagoon.

Peter was alone. The water was at his feet, and the moon was rising. For a moment he was afraid. Then he stood up straight and smiled.

“To die,” he said, “will be an awfully big adventure.”

At that moment something strange came floating towards him across the dark water.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Do You Believe in Fairies?
chapters.text:
It was the Never bird, sitting on her floating nest. She pushed it to the rock and flew away. Peter put her eggs in a hat, climbed into the nest, used his shirt as a sail, and sailed home.

Tiger Lily never forgot that Peter saved her life. After that, her people guarded the house under the ground every night.

One evening Wendy told the boys a story about a mother whose children flew away. “But the mother always left the window open,” she said, “so the children could fly back.”

Peter groaned. “Wendy, you're wrong about mothers. Long ago I flew back home. But the window was closed, and there was another little boy sleeping in my bed.”

John and Michael went white. “Wendy,” said Michael, “let's go home now!”

“Yes,” said Wendy. “We must go at once. And you can all come with us, boys. Mother and Father will love you.”

The Lost Boys cheered. But Peter only shook his head.

“I'm not going. They'll make me grow up.”

Wendy put his medicine in a cup for him and said goodbye. She was nearly crying. Peter lay down on his bed and turned his face to the wall.

Suddenly they heard terrible noises above them: shouts, the clash of swords and then silence. The pirates were attacking Tiger Lily's people!

Then a drum began to beat.

“The drum!” said the boys. “That's the sign that our friends won!”

But it was a trick. Hook was beating the drum himself. One by one the children climbed up their trees, and one by one the pirates caught them and tied them up. Wendy came last. Hook bowed to her, took her arm and walked her politely to the ship.

Then he came back alone. He looked down Peter's tree. Peter was asleep in his bed, smiling in his dreams. Hook was too big to climb down, but he could reach the cup of medicine. He took a little green bottle from his coat and poured five drops of poison into the cup. Then he crept away.

A little later Peter woke up. Tink flew in, ringing wildly.

“The pirates took Wendy and the boys!”

Peter jumped out of bed. “I'll save her! But first I'll take my medicine. Wendy wants me to.”

“No! It's poisoned!” Tink rang.

“Don't be silly. Who could poison it?”

He lifted the cup, but Tink flew between him and the cup and drank it all.

“Tink! What's wrong?”

Her light was getting weaker and weaker.

“It was poisoned,” she said softly, “and now I'm going to be dead.”

“Oh, Tink, you drank it to save me!”

But there was one way to help her. She could get better if children believed in fairies. It was night, and all over the world children were dreaming of Neverland. Peter called out to them, and to you.

“Do you believe in fairies? If you believe, clap your hands! Don't let Tink die!”

Many children clapped. A few nasty ones didn't. But it was enough. Tink's voice grew strong again, and her light became brighter than ever. In a second she was flying round the room.

Peter took his dagger.

“Hook or me this time,” he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Hook or Me
chapters.text:
On the Jolly Roger the boys stood in a line with their hands tied. Wendy was tied to the mast.

“Now, my lads,” said Hook. “Six of you will walk the plank into the sea tonight. But I need two cabin boys. Who wants to be a pirate?”

“Will we still be loyal to the King?” asked John.

“No! You must shout, 'Down with the King!'”

“Then we refuse!” cried John.

“Bring out the plank!” roared Hook.

Then they heard it. Tick-tock, tick-tock.

The pirates froze. Hook fell to his knees. “Hide me!”

But it was not the crocodile. It was Peter, ticking like a clock as he climbed onto the ship. He slipped into the dark cabin.

Hook sent a pirate in to look. There was a terrible scream, then silence. He sent another. Another scream. Soon nobody wanted to go in.

“Send in the boys!” said Hook. “Let them fight him.” The boys were pushed into the cabin, and the door closed behind them. The pirates waited.

Then the door opened, and out ran the boys, free, with swords in their hands. Peter was with them.

The fight was short. Peter cut Wendy free, and soon only Hook was left.

“Who are you, Pan?” he cried.

“I'm youth! I'm joy!” said Peter. “I'm a little bird that broke out of the egg.”

They fought up and down the ship. At last Hook climbed onto the side, ready to jump. Peter did not use his sword. He kicked him.

“Bad form!” cried Hook. A gentleman fights with a sword, not with his foot. Those were his last words. Below him, the crocodile was waiting with its mouth wide open.

The children sailed the ship home and flew the rest of the way. In London the nursery window was open. It was always open now. Mrs Darling was waiting by the fire, and Mr Darling was sleeping in Nana's kennel to punish himself for being so silly.

The children climbed into their beds. Mrs Darling looked up and saw them. She thought it was a dream. Then she held out her arms, and they ran to her.

Outside the window, Peter watched. There were many joys in his life, but this was one he could never have.

The Darlings adopted all six Lost Boys. Mrs Darling wanted to adopt Peter too.

“Would you send me to school?” he asked. “And then to an office? I'd soon be a man. No! Nobody is going to catch me and make me a man!”

He flew away, but he promised to take Wendy to Neverland once a year for spring cleaning.

Sometimes he came, and sometimes he forgot. Years passed. Wendy grew up and had a little daughter called Jane.

One night the window flew open, and there was Peter, just the same, with all his first teeth.

“Where's Wendy?” he asked. Then he saw that the tall lady by the fire was Wendy. He sat down and cried.

Jane woke up. “Boy,” she said, “why are you crying?”

Soon Jane was flying out of the window with him, and Wendy stood at the window and watched them go. She could not fly any more.

When Jane grows up, she will have a daughter too, and Peter will come for her. And so it will go on, for as long as children are young and happy and a little bit heartless.
